notes.meaning: God has just spared Nineveh, and Jonah is furious about it. The Ninevites were Assyrians, enemies of Israel, and Jonah wanted them judged. It is a strange reaction from a man who had just been shown mercy himself, rescued from the fish. Matthew Henry traces the anger to pride and hurt honor, a zeal for Israel that was not guided by real understanding.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Some early church writers praised Jonah's grief here. They compared it to Paul's love for his own people, saying he grieved because the Gentiles turning to God was a sign that Israel would be ruined.

notes.meaning: Jonah finally admits why he ran away to Tarshish. He wasn't afraid of failing. He was afraid God would forgive Nineveh. His words about God being gracious, compassionate, slow to anger and full of love come from Exodus 34:6. What all God's people praise God for, Jonah turns into a complaint. Calvin says God still counted it as a real prayer, even with its faults. "Relents from sending disaster" means God holds back punishment when people truly turn from their sin.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The NET Bible notes point out that one Hebrew word is used for Nineveh "turning" from evil and God "turning" from disaster. They say this verse is the first place the story tells us why Jonah fled in chapter 1.

notes.meaning: Jonah asks God to take his life. Elijah once prayed something similar, but he was in despair because his work seemed to fail. Jonah wants to die because his preaching worked and God spared the city. Matthew Henry calls this the language of strong feeling and folly. He also notes that a man quarreling with God is in no fit state to die. Calvin adds that our lives are in God's hands, and we should not rush toward death.

God answers with a gentle question instead of punishment. In doing so, He shows the very slowness to anger that Jonah was complaining about. Like the father in the parable of the prodigal son speaking to the older brother, God reasons with His servant. The question invites Jonah to look honestly at his own heart. It is a good question for us to ask ourselves when we get angry.

Jonah leaves the city and builds a rough hut of branches on the east side, where he can watch. Commentators differ on the timing. Many think the forty days were already over, but Jonah still hoped some judgment might fall. Matthew Henry notes that people with fretful spirits often make trouble for themselves, so they always have something to complain about.

God kindly gives His sulking servant a fast-growing plant for shade. No one knows for sure what plant it was. Many think it was the castor-oil plant with its large leaves. This is the first time Jonah is happy in the book, but his joy is as self-centered as his anger was. A small gift at the right time can be a real blessing. Still, we should not make earthly comforts our greatest joy.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Some early church writers read the plant as a picture of Israel's Old Testament promises and privileges, a shadow of better things to come.

notes.meaning: The next morning God sends a worm that kills the plant. The book keeps saying God "appointed" things: the fish, the plant, the worm and the wind. He is in charge of every detail. Calvin says even a worm's chewing is guided by God. Matthew Henry notes how quickly earthly comforts can wither, often from some small cause we never see.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Some early church writers saw the "morning worm" as a picture of Christ, who says "I am a worm" in Psalm 22. In this reading, the gospel made Israel's old privileges wither.

notes.meaning: God sends a hot, dry east wind, and the sun beats down on Jonah until he feels faint. Once again he wishes he were dead. He had been overjoyed by the plant and now he is crushed by its loss. Calvin notes he doesn't say he prayed this time. Matthew Henry gives this comfort: when our "plant" is gone, our God is not gone.

God asks again whether Jonah has any right to be angry, this time about the plant. Jonah digs in and says yes, angry enough to die. Calvin sees how stubborn even a true prophet can become when he feeds his feelings. Matthew Henry notes that speaking wrongly is bad, but standing by it is worse. These are Jonah's last recorded words, but they are not the last words of the book.

God uses Jonah's own feelings to teach him. Jonah felt sorry for a plant he never planted, watered or made grow. It sprang up quickly and died just as quickly. If Jonah cared that much about a short-lived plant, he had little reason for his anger over the city.

God makes His point: if Jonah pitied a plant, how much more should God care for a great city of people He made and kept alive? Most commentators take "cannot tell their right hand from their left" as meaning young children, more than 120,000 of them. They had not earned the city's punishment. God even cares about the animals. The book ends with God's question and no reply from Jonah. It teaches that God's mercy reaches people of every nation, not just one's own group.

differ.view: Some evangelicals take "cannot tell their right hand from their left" to mean people unable to make moral judgments, not only young children.
